lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you met idioms. What does "a piece of cake" mean? Very easy: its meaning isn't in its words.
Idioms are sayings whose meaning isn't in the words: "Hold your horses" means wait. No horses are needed!
Proverbs and adages are old sayings with advice: "Look before you leap" means think before you act.
To work one out, think about the situation it is used in.
Some more: once in a blue moon (very rarely), under the weather (a bit ill), the early bird catches the worm (starting early helps).

Try it in the world: when you and a friend build together, say "Two heads are better than one!" Find a moment for another proverb too, like look before you leap by a cliff. Next: words with two meanings.

exercises.prompt: "Hold your horses!" What does it mean?
exercises.hint: It is said to someone rushing.
exercises.explain: It means wait a moment.

exercises.prompt: "I feel under the weather." What does it mean?
exercises.hint: It is about how you feel.
choices: I am out in the rain.
exercises.explain: It means feeling a bit ill.

exercises.prompt: "Once in a blue moon" means very rarely.
exercises.hint: Blue moons are rare.
exercises.explain: Yes: it means very rarely.

exercises.prompt: "Look before you leap." What is the advice?
exercises.hint: It is about being careful.
exercises.explain: Think before you act.

exercises.prompt: Which is a proverb?
exercises.hint: A saying with advice.
choices: The early bird catches the worm.
exercises.explain: It gives advice: starting early helps.

exercises.prompt: "She let the cat out of the bag." What does it mean?
exercises.hint: It is about a secret.
choices: She told a secret by mistake.
exercises.explain: It means she let a secret slip.

exercises.prompt: "Don't cry over spilt milk." What is the advice?
exercises.hint: Can spilt milk go back in the glass?
choices: Don't be upset about what can't be changed.
exercises.explain: It means don't worry about what's done.

exercises.prompt: "We're in the same boat." What does it mean?
exercises.hint: Think of two friends with the same trouble.
exercises.explain: It means we share the same situation.

exercises.prompt: "Hit the books" means to study hard.
exercises.hint: It isn't about hitting.
exercises.explain: Yes: it means study hard.

exercises.prompt: "Two heads are better than one." What is the advice?
exercises.hint: Imagine two friends working on one puzzle. Is it easier than alone?
exercises.explain: Two people can solve a problem better than one.

exercises.prompt: Before the fair, Mum says, "Don't put all your eggs in one basket." What does she mean?
exercises.hint: What if the one basket falls?
choices: Don't rely on just one plan.
exercises.explain: It means have more than one plan.

exercises.prompt: Sam says his brother "has a heart of gold". What is his brother like?
exercises.hint: It is about his heart, not money.
exercises.explain: A heart of gold means very kind.

exercises.prompt: Nia practised every day and at last played the song perfectly. Which proverb fits?
exercises.hint: What did Nia do every day?
exercises.explain: She practised and got it perfect.

exercises.prompt: "Every cloud has a silver lining" means bad things always happen.
exercises.hint: It is a hopeful saying.
exercises.explain: No: it means something good can come even from a bad time.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean to "break the ice" at a party?
exercises.hint: At first, nobody at the party is talking. What does breaking the ice do?
exercises.explain: It means getting people chatting.

exercises.prompt: Match each idiom to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Think of when people say each one.
exercises.explain: Under the weather: a bit ill. Hold your horses: wait a moment. Once in a blue moon: very rarely. Hit the books: study hard.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sayings: idiom or proverb (a saying with advice)?
items: two heads are better than one
exercises.hint: Does it give advice about how to live, or is it just a colourful way to say something?
exercises.explain: A piece of cake, under the weather and hold your horses are idioms. Look before you leap, practice makes perfect and two heads are better than one give advice: proverbs.

exercises.prompt: Match each proverb to its advice.
items: Two heads are better than one.
The early bird catches the worm.
exercises.hint: Picture each saying as a real scene, then ask what lesson it teaches.
exercises.explain: Look before you leap: think before you act. Two heads: work together. The early bird: starting early helps. Spilt milk: don't fret about what can't be changed.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the saying that fits it.
items: Ava rushes at a cliff edge
Sam is a bit ill today
matches: two heads are better than one
let the cat out of the bag
exercises.hint: Think about what is happening in each situation, then find the saying used for it.
exercises.explain: Telling a secret by mistake: let the cat out of the bag. Rushing at a cliff: look before you leap. A bit ill: under the weather. Solving it together: two heads are better than one.

exercises.prompt: Work out what an idiom means: put the steps in order.
items: Notice the plain words make no sense.
exercises.hint: Card 3 says to think about the situation the saying is used in. What comes before that?
exercises.explain: Read the whole sentence, notice that the plain words make no sense (no cat in a bag!), think about the situation, then choose the meaning that fits it.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: is the saying used the right way?
items: Ava was under the weather, so she stayed in bed.
It's a piece of cake, so it took all day.
We see snow once in a blue moon here.
Hold your horses, run as fast as you can!
exercises.hint: Swap each saying for its meaning, then read the sentence again. Does it make sense?
exercises.explain: Right: under the weather (a bit ill), so she stayed in bed; snow comes very rarely. Not right: a piece of cake means easy, not all day; hold your horses means wait, not run.

exercises.prompt: Match each saying to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Think of the situation each one is used in: a party, a friend, a problem, a test.
exercises.explain: Break the ice: get people talking. A heart of gold: very kind. In the same boat: sharing the same problem. Hit the books: study hard.
